name: Cold Chillin' Records
ownershipStory: Started in 1986 by Tyrone Williams, who managed the Juice Crew, and Len Fichtelberg, whose Prism Records it absorbed. It was the Juice Crew's label, with Marley Marl as its in-house producer, and released Biz Markie, Big Daddy Kane, Roxanne Shanté and MC Shan. A five-year distribution deal with Warner Bros. ran from 1988 to 1993. In December 1991 a federal court ruled against Warner over a sample on a Biz Markie album the label had released without permission, and the album was pulled from sale. The label was defunct by 1998.
hook: The Juice Crew's label, and the one that lost the court case that made every hip-hop sample something you have to pay for.
blurb: Cold Chillin' was the label for the Juice Crew, the group of rappers around producer Marley Marl in Queensbridge. In 1991 it put out a Biz Markie album with a song built on a piece of Gilbert O'Sullivan's 1972 hit. Biz had asked O'Sullivan for permission and been told no, and the label released it anyway. O'Sullivan sued and won, in Grand Upright Music v. Warner Bros. Records (S.D.N.Y., 17 December 1991), and the album was pulled from the shops. The ruling ended the time when hip-hop producers could treat recorded music as free material. From then on anyone who wanted to sample a record had to ask first and usually pay, so clearing samples became a legal and budget line on every record, and the dense collages of the late 1980s became too expensive to make. The label's own collapse came later and is not blamed on the case here.
